name: Clobetasol propionate
lead: Clobetasol propionate is a super-high-potency topical corticosteroid, the top group in the seven-class US potency ranking [1][2]. It is prescribed for corticosteroid-responsive skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, and as a treatment for cutaneous graft-versus-host disease [1][2].

Its relevance to appearance is as an undeclared or illicit ingredient in skin-lightening creams. Wikipedia reports that it is used cosmetically for skin whitening, that the FDA has not approved it for that purpose, and that products containing it are sold internationally and online, in some cases at higher concentrations than prescription products allow [2]. A 2016 study cited there ranks it, with mercury and hydroquinone, among the most toxic and most-used lightening agents [2].

The US label restricts use to short courses and a maximum weekly amount because the drug can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis [1]. No clinical trials have tested clobetasol as a skin-lightening treatment; its documented trial evidence concerns inflammatory skin disease. The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of it.

paras: The US label describes it as indicated for relief of the inflammatory and itching manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses [1]. Wikipedia lists eczema, contact dermatitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis (including scalp and plaque), lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, alopecia areata, mycosis fungoides and cutaneous graft-versus-host disease, in cream, foam, gel, solution, ointment and shampoo forms [2].

Wikipedia reports that the drug is used for skin whitening, describes this as controversial, and notes that lightening creams containing it are found in some New York City beauty-supply stores and online [2]. Reported effects of such use include thinning, easily bruised skin, visible capillaries, acne, permanent stretch marks, high blood pressure, raised blood sugar and suppression of the body's natural steroids [2].

In label trials, the most frequent adverse events were burning, irritation and itching in about 0.5% of treated patients; less frequent reactions included stinging, cracking, redness, folliculitis, skin atrophy and telangiectasia, and Cushing's syndrome has been reported in infants and adults [1]. Wikipedia adds cellulitis, adrenal suppression and allergic reactions among serious effects [2]. A 1989 case report describes clobetasol-induced milia [3].

The label advises against treatment beyond two consecutive weeks and against exceeding 50 g a week because of the potential to suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis [1]. Corticosteroids have been teratogenic in animals at relatively low systemic doses, clobetasol has not been tested for teratogenicity topically, and it is absorbed through the skin [1].
Clobetasol propionate is a synthetic glucocorticoid ester (ATC code D07AD01) that is believed to act by activating steroid receptors [2].

Wikipedia reports that it was patented in 1968 and entered medical use in 1978 and is available as a generic; in 2023 it was the 129th most commonly prescribed medicine in the US, with more than 4 million prescriptions [2].

A 1975 double-blind trial in 34 patients with psoriasis vulgaris found clobetasol propionate cream more effective than betamethasone valerate cream over two weeks, and 14 of 16 patients who had not responded to betamethasone valerate ointment improved quickly after switching [4]. A randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial examined clobetasol 0.05% for oral lichen planus [5]. Registered trials include clobetasol shampoo maintenance in scalp psoriasis (288 participants), spray versus foam and ointment comparisons in psoriasis, and an ophthalmic nanoemulsion after cataract surgery [6][7][8].
No studies found of clobetasol as a skin-lightening treatment.

card.summary: A super-potent prescription steroid that turns up in illicit lightening creams; its documented skin harms are significant.
card.note: Not approved for lightening; label limits use to 2 weeks and 50 g a week due to adrenal suppression.

quick.overview:
Clobetasol propionate is the strongest class of topical corticosteroid, prescribed for psoriasis, eczema, lichen conditions and similar. It is also reported as an ingredient in illicit skin-lightening creams, which is not an approved use.

No trials have tested it for lightening, and the sources contain no forum discussion of it.
quick.mechanism: It activates glucocorticoid receptors in the skin, dampening inflammation.
quick.risks: Reported effects include skin thinning, bruising, visible capillaries, stretch marks, acne, raised blood pressure and blood sugar, and adrenal suppression; Cushing's syndrome has been reported. The label limits use to two weeks and 50 g per week, and it is prescription-only in the US.
